observation: Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas (2019) reframe germane load as a redistribution mechanism: capacity freed by reducing extraneous load flows into intrinsic processing of the same material, rather than being a separate additive resource pool.
claim: Reducing extraneous UI load and aiding comprehension are the same lever, not competing budgets, in Riemann's design.
mechanism: Working memory capacity is a shared pool; anything not spent parsing chrome/clutter is automatically available for processing the content itself.
population: general learners (theoretical synthesis of CLT experimental base)
context: theoretical position paper, not a new empirical study

implications.text: Treat chrome minimalism as a direct lever on comprehension, not a stylistic trade-off against it, when designing the zoom-dial UI.

observation: The expertise-reversal effect is best explained as a special case of the general element-interactivity effect: what changes with expertise is how many raw elements must be held in working memory to interpret one chunk, since experts have pre-compiled schemas novices lack.
claim: A fixed level of detail is necessarily miscalibrated for either novices (too dense) or experts (too sparse) on the same content; a continuous, per-session-adjustable dial is the correct design primitive rather than a binary simplified/full toggle.
mechanism: Experts' pre-compiled schemas let them treat several raw elements as one chunk, lowering effective element interactivity for the same content relative to a novice.
context: decades of replicated CLT experiments plus a 2025 meta-analysis

implications.text: Implement the zoom dial as a continuous, per-session-settable control rather than a fixed simplified/full toggle; let familiarity with this specific document (not just general domain expertise) push the default dial position higher.

observation: A 2024/2025 meta-analysis (92 articles/181 studies/591 effects) of Mayer's extraneous-processing principles finds pooled effect g~0.37 with shrinkage over study-year; specific modern estimates: contiguity g~0.74, multimedia g~0.39, signalling g~0.38, segmenting g~0.32-0.36, coherence/seductive-details g~-0.37 to -0.41 (irrelevant detail measurably hurts).
claim: Spatial/temporal contiguity, signalling, and excluding seductive irrelevant detail all have real, replicated (if smaller-than-classic) effects on comprehension.
mechanism: Contiguity avoids split-attention between related pieces of information; signalling cues structure without adding content; excluding seductive detail avoids competing for limited attention with the load-bearing content.

implications.text: Instruct the summariser to actively exclude engaging-but-irrelevant colour/anecdote from L0-L2, not just compress for length.
Visually cue each abstraction level's own structure (e.g. bold the claim-bearing clause of a gist).
Keep the anchored passage at the viewport centre across zoom transitions (spatial/temporal contiguity), since this is one of the largest and most consistent effects found.
Never show the L1 gist and a synchronized highlight of the identical sentence in L3 simultaneously on screen (redundancy).

observation: Preattentive attributes (Ware: form/colour/position/motion; Healey: 16 cues) are processed in under ~200-250ms, before conscious/serial visual search.
claim: A small, consistent preattentive vocabulary (one hue/luminance step per level, a consistent depth-indent) can mark zoom level/structure at near-zero reading-attention cost.
mechanism: Preattentive features are detected by low-level parallel visual processing before conscious attention engages, so they don't compete with reading comprehension for the same attentional channel.
context: decades of replicated perceptual-science lab studies

implications.text: Use a single hue/luminance step and consistent left-margin depth-indent to mark tree depth/zoom level, plus a brief motion pulse only for newly-arrived content while streaming.

observation: Rosenholtz's Feature Congestion and Subband Entropy metrics give quantifiable, human-validated measures of visual clutter, computable on arbitrary images (open-source implementation exists).
claim: Visual clutter is a measurable quantity Riemann can compute at build/render time, not just a matter of aesthetic judgment.
context: peer-reviewed vision science, replicated as a working metric in HCI

implications.text: Programmatically clutter-score each rendered level and auto-collapse or paginate when an L2 view crosses a clutter threshold, rather than rendering everything flat.

observation: Tufte's data-ink-ratio/chartjunk framework is contested: at least one controlled study (Inbar & Tractinsky) found users preferred non-minimalist, decorated bar graphs over maximal-data-ink versions.
claim: Maximising data-ink ratio is not a universally preference-optimizing rule; 'clean minimalist' is a style choice, not a proven cognitive-load win, and should not override measured clutter scores or expert-user density preferences.
context: lab, controlled preference study contradicting the popular heuristic

implications.text: Tie any minimalism decision to the measured Rosenholtz clutter score rather than to the data-ink heuristic as an end in itself; a slightly warmer/less austere rendering is not evidence-contradicted.

observation: Optimal line length is commonly cited as ~50-75 characters per line (Bringhurst 45-75, ~66 most-cited); very short lines increase costly saccade/return-sweep frequency, very long lines make it harder to track the correct next line.
claim: Riemann should cap the markdown prose column at roughly 60-75 characters for L1-L3, regardless of abstraction level (L0's one-liner is short enough this doesn't apply).
mechanism: Line length affects the frequency and accuracy of return-sweep eye movements between the end of one line and the start of the next.
population: general readers (screen and print reading studies)
context: literature review synthesising heterogeneous older studies

implications.text: Set a max-width content column of roughly 60-75 characters for L1-L3 rendered prose.

observation: A 2026 meta-analysis (15 studies, 91 effect sizes, N=688) found dyslexia-specific fonts (OpenDyslexic, Dyslexie) have no reliable benefit to reading speed or accuracy versus standard fonts; one study found OpenDyslexic actually reduced speed/accuracy vs Arial/Times. Increased letter/word spacing does have supporting evidence.
claim: Adding a dedicated dyslexia-font mode as an accessibility feature would not deliver a real comprehension win; generous letter/line spacing and line-length control are the better-evidenced levers.

implications.text: Do not add an OpenDyslexic/dyslexia-font toggle expecting a comprehension benefit; offer spacing and line-length controls instead if targeting neurodivergent readers.

observation: NN/g's original F-shaped scanning pattern (2006 eye-tracking, 232 users) is now understood by NN/g's own follow-up research as a failure state emerging from content lacking clear headings/hierarchy; well-structured content instead produces a 'layer-cake' pattern where fixations land on headings/subheadings with occasional dips into body text.
claim: L2 section gists should render as genuinely distinct headed blocks with short (40-80 word) bodies, front-loading the claim in the first clause, so a layer-cake scanner reading only headings and first clauses still gets the gist's payload.
mechanism: Clear heading hierarchy lets a reader's scan pattern efficiently sample the structure without needing to serially read body prose.
population: general web readers (232-user eye-tracking study plus follow-up)
context: large-sample eye-tracking lab study with a direct named follow-up correction

implications.text: Render L2 as headed blocks with 40-80 word bodies, with the claim front-loaded in the first clause.

observation: Categorical colour distinguishability drops steeply between 5 and 6 simultaneous categories; practitioner/CVD-safety guidance converges on capping categorical palettes around 5-7 hues with adequate lightness separation, and never using colour as the sole encoding channel.
claim: If Riemann ever colour-codes tree depth or zoom level, it should use at most ~5 distinct hues and always co-encode with a redundant channel (position on the dial, an explicit level label).
context: perceptual/visualization research plus CVD-safety design guidance

implications.text: Cap any level/depth colour coding at <=5 hues and always pair colour with position/label, never colour alone.

observation: Heer & Robertson (2007) found animated transitions between related chart states aid 'object constancy' -- preserving a viewer's tracking of an object's identity across a representational change -- versus an instant cut that forces re-orientation from scratch.
claim: Animating the zoom dial's level transitions (even a short 150-250ms reflow/fade) supports the anchoring requirement by keeping the anchored passage visibly 'the same thing' as it changes representation, but should fall back to an instant cut for prefers-reduced-motion.
mechanism: Smooth animated transitions let the visual system track an element's continuity through a state change rather than treating before/after as two unrelated scenes.
context: highly cited, replicated InfoVis lab research; original context is charts, not reflowing text blocks

implications.text: Animate level transitions briefly (~150-250ms scroll/fade) rather than snapping instantly, with an instant-cut fallback under prefers-reduced-motion that preserves anchor position via scroll offset alone.

observation: Practitioner sources report interface-density preference is expertise/frequency-dependent: experts and frequent users perform better with denser, well-organised layouts, while novices/casual users need sparser ones; well-organized density and poor organization are framed as different axes, not opposite ends of one 'clean vs dense' spectrum.
claim: Riemann's default dial position and chrome density should key off measured familiarity/expertise with this specific tree (has the user zoomed this doc before, how many docs this week), not a single global simple/power-user toggle.
context: UX-practitioner sources/design blogs, not controlled academic density studies

implications.text: Key default dial position and chrome density to measured familiarity/session recency on the specific document, extending the brief's 'adaptive load scaling' principle with a concrete trigger.

observation: Notification/interruption research shows merely suppressing the urge to respond to a visible notification consumes attentional resources even with zero interaction; interruptions early in a task are more likely to cause complete loss of the task goal than interruptions late in a task; task-relevant interruptions are markedly less disruptive than irrelevant ones; adaptive peripheral-to-central escalation reduces workload versus fixed always-central alerts.
claim: Any Riemann notification (e.g. 'L1 is ready') should be a peripheral, non-modal cue that never interrupts an active L3 read unless directly relevant to what's on screen, and should especially avoid interrupting near the start of a session.
mechanism: Interruption cost comes partly from context-reconstruction after the interrupt, and partly from ongoing suppression of the urge to attend to a visible cue, both of which are worse early in a task before context is consolidated.
population: general knowledge workers (interruption-science literature); adaptive-placement finding from a single MR study
context: mix of established interruption-science lab/field studies and one novel-modality single study

implications.text: Make any Riemann-initiated surfacing (e.g. 'L1 ready') a small peripheral badge, never a focus-stealing popup, and suppress it entirely during an active read of directly-related content.

observation: A 2026 Springer comparison and related 2025 studies converge on a genuine trade-off: light mode supports objectively faster reading and lower cognitive workload; dark mode wins on subjective visual comfort/eye strain, especially in low light or extended sessions, with majority user preference for dark mode despite the performance edge going the other way.
claim: There is no single 'right' theme default; light and dark mode trade performance against comfort, and theme is a plausible adaptive signal (time of day, session length, read depth) rather than a fixed accessible choice.

implications.text: Respect OS prefers-color-scheme by default; treat theme as a candidate adaptive signal, defaulting to light for a deep effortful L3 read and allowing dark for low-energy/low-light browsing sessions.
